clue.text: Parasite acted as Prime Minister, according to Spooner

indicators.note: Dr Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of a pair of words, so his version exchanges them

blocks.note: the Prime Minister leads the House of Commons, so someone acting as one led the House; swap the opening sounds

explanation.surface: An insult: some bloodsucking politician who once held the top job.
explanation.walkthrough: LED HOUSE with its first sounds exchanged becomes the answer. The House is the House of Commons, the British parliament's elected chamber.
explanation.definitionFit: A head louse is a small wingless insect living in human hair and feeding on blood, a textbook parasite.

clue.text: Killer – popular song starts to make Adamski notable

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only the initials are kept

blocks.note: a hit is a song that sells well
initials of the three words

explanation.surface: Adamski's chart hit was called Killer; the clue imagines a big song making the musician famous.
explanation.walkthrough: Adamski is a British electronic musician whose 1990 single Killer reached number one, which is why the surface feels so natural.
explanation.definitionFit: A hitman is a professional assassin hired to murder people, so he is a killer by trade.

clue.text: Adult keen, say, with vigorous speed cut material

indicators.note: a cut word has been trimmed, here losing its final letter

blocks.note: A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult
to keen is to wail in grief, an example of crying
LICK, a fast pace as in 'at a lick', without its last letter

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic grown-up cutting cloth at great speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' looks like an adjective meaning eager, but here it is the verb to lament; 'say' flags it as one example of crying.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrylic is a synthetic fibre and the fabric woven from it, so it is a kind of cloth or textile.

clue.text: Can you see orator that’s rich?

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: observe the person who is speaking
second meaning: a retort accusing someone of hypocrisy

explanation.walkthrough: The question seems to be about spotting a speaker, and 'that's rich' seems to describe a wealthy one; both halves are really ways of saying the same stock phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is said when a critic is guilty of the same fault, exactly as the sarcastic retort 'that's rich' is used.

clue.text: Extreme mullets regularly seen on soldiers

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: second, fourth and sixth letters
RA is the Royal Artillery

explanation.surface: Soldiers sporting an extreme haircut, short at the front and long at the back.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue one piece is 'on' another when it sits above it. A mullet is a hairstyle, which is what the surface suggests, but also a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultra as an adjective or prefix means going beyond the usual limits, as in ultra-conservative views.

clue.text: Cooking himself, the man setting aside fish prepared cheese

indicators.note: cooking mixes and transforms ingredients, so these letters are stirred into a new order
to set something aside is to remove it from the pile, so some letters are taken out

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, letters to remove

explanation.surface: A man busy in the kitchen, leaving the fish aside and making cheese instead.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove F, I, S and H from the thirteen letters, wherever they fall, and rearrange the nine left. 'Prepared' joins wordplay to definition, saying the process made the cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Emmenthal is a hard Swiss cheese with large holes, so it is one type of cheese.

clue.text: Not completely unassuming object

indicators.note: something not complete lacks a part, here its final letter

blocks.note: DEMURE, meaning modest, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Something that is not entirely modest, perhaps an ornament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' reads as a noun, a thing, but it is the verb meaning to protest.
explanation.definitionFit: To demur is to raise objections or show reluctance, so it matches the verb sense of protesting.

clue.text: Description of Day-Lewis’s stunt replacement stowed in vessel

blocks.note: a stunt double stands in for an actor
put into a barrel

explanation.surface: Daniel Day-Lewis, the actor, needs a stuntman; the clue seems to describe that replacement being stashed on a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The actor's name suggests the stunt double, but the definition refers to his hyphenated surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A surname made of two joined parts linked by a hyphen, like Day-Lewis, is commonly called double-barrelled.

clue.text: Name of woman borne by camel is Sarah

indicators.note: something borne is carried inside, so the letters ride within the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across these words

explanation.surface: A camel's rider, named in the desert scene, is a woman called Sarah.
explanation.walkthrough: Sarah looks like the woman's name the clue wants, but the answer sits inside the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Melissa is a common female first name, so it is a name a woman can have.

clue.text: Call on team close to match

blocks.note: to ring is to telephone
a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: A manager phoning the squad near the end of a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to match' sounds like the final minutes of a game, but 'close' means near, as in the seats beside a boxing ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Ringside seats are those right beside a boxing ring, so they put spectators near the fight.

clue.text: Number of people in attendance switch off

blocks.note: first meaning: the count of those who come to an event
second meaning: to extinguish a light, written as two words

explanation.surface: So many people came that someone was asked to kill the lights.
explanation.walkthrough: The noun is one word and the phrasal verb is two, which the single enumeration hides.
explanation.definitionFit: Election turnout is how many voters came, while turning out a lamp means extinguishing it.

clue.text: Tearful graduate rejected love of the Parisian

indicators.note: rejected things are sent back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: MA is a Master of Arts
love is a zero score in tennis, and nil is zero
du is French for 'of the'

explanation.surface: A graduate weeping after being turned down by the Parisian they loved.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the last two pieces turn round together; the graduate stays at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Maudlin means self-pityingly sentimental and weepy, often from drink, so it is a near synonym.

clue.text: Shining silver base

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
base in the sense of low or mean

explanation.surface: A gleaming silver stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' looks like a noun, the stand of a trophy, but it is the adjective meaning lowly.
explanation.definitionFit: Something aglow is glowing and radiant with light, so it is gleaming brightly.

clue.text: Heard those testing recorders

indicators.note: what is heard is what reaches the ear, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: analysts examine and test things

explanation.surface: Someone overheard the people trying out recorders, perhaps in a music shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recorders' suggests the musical instrument or tape machines; here it means people who keep records.
explanation.definitionFit: An annalist writes annals, a yearly chronicle of events, so is a keeper of historical records.

clue.text: How chess opponents see each other is affecting everyone

definitions.text: How chess opponents see each other

blocks.clueFragment: How chess opponents see each other
blocks.note: first meaning, literal: facing each other over the chequered playing surface
second meaning: applying to all without exception

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a literal reading of a phrase whose usual sense is the second, as with across-the-board pay rises.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes measures that apply equally to all members of a group, such as universal cuts.

clue.text: Spoiled goat’s beard tidied up with no resistance

indicators.note: to be with no item is to lack it, so a letter is dropped
tidying rearranges things into a new order, so the letters are reshuffled

blocks.note: GOATSBEARD with its R removed
R is the physics symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: An unkempt goat's beard was trimmed without complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: Goat's beard is also a wildflower, but only its letters matter here.
explanation.definitionFit: To sabotage is to wreck deliberately, so something sabotaged has been ruined or spoilt.

clue.text: Cops, ones arresting jerk endlessly

indicators.note: to arrest is to seize and hold, so one piece holds another
without an end, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: an ace counts as one on dice and cards
QUIRK, a sudden twist or turn, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Police officers detaining an idiot, over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cops' looks like the noun for police, but it is the slang verb, as in copping a fine.
explanation.definitionFit: To cop something is informal for getting or obtaining it, so cops means gets hold of.

clue.text: Law enforcement groups displaying “Fraud’s unacceptable” on front of large sign

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: a con is a fraud, plus the 's
a variant spelling of taboo
its first letter
Aries is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: Police forces putting up a big poster warning that fraud will not be tolerated.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted slogan looks like one phrase but splits into a noun with its 's and an adjective. A British county police force is formally called a constabulary.
explanation.definitionFit: A constabulary is a police force covering a district, so several are law enforcement bodies.

clue.text: Not so confident approach ignoring a rival

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: NEAR, to come close, without its A
the letter to drop
a vier is one who vies, a competitor

explanation.surface: Someone losing nerve as they face an opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: VIER is rare outside crosswords: anyone who vies with another, so a rival.
explanation.definitionFit: Nervier is the comparative of nervy, meaning anxious or jumpy, so describes someone less assured.

clue.text: Stone mass circumvented by leader at sea

indicators.note: being at sea means confused and lost, so the letters are jumbled
to be circumvented is to be gone round, so one piece is surrounded

blocks.note: its letters rearranged
m is the symbol for mass

explanation.surface: A captain at sea, sailing round a great block of rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader at sea' reads as a ship's captain; 'at sea' is really the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An emerald is a green precious gem, and stone is the usual term for a jewel.

clue.text: Strong shelter put up in animal pen

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting up means raising, so the letters read bottom to top
being inside means one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: the lee is the sheltered side, away from the wind
a pigsty

explanation.surface: A sturdy shelter built inside a farm enclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' in the surface means built, as one puts up a shed.
explanation.definitionFit: Steely means hard and resolute like steel, so it describes firm strength or determination.

clue.text: Independent manner ultimately displeased hosts

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter counts
a host takes in a guest, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: not elated, so unhappy
its final letter

explanation.surface: A self-reliant attitude that, in the end, annoyed the people throwing a party.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'displeased hosts' as unhappy party-givers; in fact 'hosts' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Unrelated things have no connection to each other, so each one stands apart and separate.

clue.text: Dialect of doctor entertaining scientific group

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to have them in, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: a familiar term for a doctor
the RI is the Royal Institution, a British science body

explanation.surface: A physician addressing a science society in his own regional accent.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Institution is a London body that promotes science, famous for its Christmas lectures.
explanation.definitionFit: Doric is the broad Scots speech of north-east Scotland, so it is a regional dialect.

clue.text: Not odd time for competition

blocks.note: a number that is not odd is even
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Nothing strange about it: it is just the hour to compete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not odd' seems to mean normal, but it is the opposite of odd in numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: An event is a single contest within a sports meeting, such as the hundred metres.

clue.text: Sacking on article splits

indicators.note: to split something is to break into it, so a piece is lodged in the middle

blocks.note: riding as in being carried, like a passenger on a horse
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about losing one's job, split up for publication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacking' suggests dismissal from work, but here it is plundering a town; 'on' is the hardest step, riding as one rides on a bus.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacking a city means plundering it, and raiding is attacking a place to seize its goods.

clue.text: Issue about tenure

blocks.note: re means concerning
a lease is a period of holding property

explanation.surface: A problem concerning someone's job security or property rights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' reads as a noun, a problem, but it is the verb to put out.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue a record or statement is to publish it or put it out, which is to release it.

clue.text: Small piece of material circling around neck

indicators.note: circling something means going all round it, so it ends up enclosed

blocks.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
a rag is a scrap of cloth
c stands for circa, Latin for around

explanation.surface: A little scarf or ribbon wrapped round someone's throat.
explanation.walkthrough: The small letter and the rag together go round C; 'around' is not a second wrapping signal but the abbreviation used with dates.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrag is an old informal word for the neck, also the bony neck end of mutton sold by butchers.

clue.text: Clearly play second fiddle to marshal, abandoning plans of rebelling

indicators.note: to marshal troops is to arrange them in order, so the letters are rearranged
abandoning something means leaving it behind, so those letters are removed
rebels refuse to stay in line, so the letters removed may appear in any order

blocks.note: taken as written, sixteen letters
taken as written, seven letters to remove

explanation.surface: Plainly accept a subordinate role to the officer in charge, giving up any rebel schemes.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of 'plans of' out of 'play second fiddle', wherever they fall, and rearrange the nine left. The phrase reads like an idiom to define, but it is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Decidedly means unquestionably or in a definite manner, so it works as an adverb like plainly.
